title: Central Italy's Rare Grapes in Depth
quiz.0.question: What is the historic place of Vernaccia di San Gimignano in Italian wine law?
quiz.0.options.0: The first white wine to receive DOCG status (1993)
quiz.0.options.1: Italy's first wine to receive DOC status (1966), later promoted to DOCG
quiz.0.options.2: The first Italian white to appear at international auction
quiz.0.options.3: The first Italian wine to enter the US market
quiz.0.explanation: Vernaccia di San Gimignano became Italy's first DOC wine in 1966 and was promoted to DOCG in 1993 — a landmark appellation in the history of Italian wine law.
quiz.1.question: Where is Ciliegiolo mainly grown?
quiz.1.options.1: The Maremma coast of Toscana and Umbria
quiz.1.options.2: The volcanic hills of southern Campania
quiz.1.explanation: Ciliegiolo (Italian for "little cherry") is grown mainly on the Maremma coast of southern Toscana (Maremma Toscana DOC) and in Umbria. Known for vivid wild cherry and rose aromas, it was traditionally a small part of Chianti blends.
quiz.2.question: Cesanese del Piglio is a traditional speciality of which city?
quiz.2.explanation: Cesanese del Piglio DOCG is a traditional red from the province of Frosinone, south-east of Rome. It is said to have been loved by the papal court and the Roman nobility, is the most common local red in traditional Roman trattorias, and is Lazio's most important red grape.
quiz.3.question: What is the biggest stylistic difference between Vernaccia di San Gimignano and Verdicchio?
quiz.3.options.1: Vernaccia is known for its slightly bitter finish and minerality, Verdicchio for high acidity and almond flavours
quiz.3.options.2: Vernaccia is a red grape, Verdicchio a white grape
quiz.3.options.3: The two are almost identical in style
quiz.3.explanation: Vernaccia di San Gimignano's signature is a slightly bitter finish (almond bitterness) and minerality; Verdicchio di Matelica is known for crisp high acidity, fresh green apple and a distinctive bitter-almond finish — both have a bitter-almond element, but expressed differently.
quiz.4.question: What role does Colorino play in Chianti Classico?
quiz.4.options.0: The main grape, over 80% of the blend
quiz.4.options.1: A supporting blending grape providing deep colour and structure
quiz.4.options.2: A white grape giving fresh acidity
quiz.4.options.3: It is banned from Chianti Classico
quiz.4.explanation: Colorino (Italian for "the one that gives colour") is a traditional Tuscan blending grape. Its deep colour (almost purple-black) and rich tannins give Chianti blends depth of colour and structure, usually at 5-10% of the blend.
quiz.5.question: How has the natural-wine movement affected Ciliegiolo?
quiz.5.options.0: It led to Ciliegiolo being banned from commercial production
quiz.5.options.1: Natural producers saw Ciliegiolo's potential for character and let it shine through low intervention, helping its revival
quiz.5.options.2: It turned Ciliegiolo into a sparkling-wine grape
quiz.5.options.3: It has had almost no effect on Ciliegiolo
quiz.5.explanation: The natural-wine movement favours low intervention and no added sulphur, letting a grape's personality show fully — Ciliegiolo's bright wild berries and rose aromas stand out especially under low-intervention winemaking, helping it move from "supporting grape" to "lead grape".
quiz.6.question: Among Central Italy's rare grapes, which holds a "first" in Italian wine law and is known for a slightly bitter finish?
quiz.6.explanation: Vernaccia di San Gimignano was the first wine recognised under Italy's DOC law (1966) and is known for its slightly bitter almond finish and minerality; it is one of Toscana's most important white grapes.
slides.0.title: Central Italy's Rare Grapes in Depth
slides.0.subtitle: Vernaccia · Ciliegiolo · Cesanese · Verdicchio · Colorino — forgotten pearls from Toscana to Lazio
slides.1.title: Vernaccia di San Gimignano — Italy's First DOC
slides.1.content:
A Legal Milestone: Where Italy's DOC System Began

When Italy introduced its DOC wine law in 1966, Vernaccia di San Gimignano became the first wine in the whole country to receive DOC status. It was promoted to DOCG in 1993, confirming its historic place among Italian whites. This "first" is not just an honour: it is a witness to the birth of Italy's entire wine-law system.

1966: Italy's first DOC | 1993: promoted to DOCG | Origin: San Gimignano, the town of stone towers, Toscana

Grape Profile

Colour: pale gold, sometimes with green tints
Aromas: white flowers (acacia), orange blossom, white peach, stone, a hint of pineapple | with age: beeswax, toast, mushroom
Palate signature: a distinctive slightly bitter finish (almond-skin bitterness) + a mineral aftertaste — Vernaccia's most recognisable flavour fingerprint
Structure: medium body, crisp acidity, suited to drinking young (1-5 years); Riserva is aged at least 11 months (including 3 in bottle) and can age 5-10 years
slides.2.title: Vernaccia in Depth: Producers and Schools of Style
slides.2.content:
Modern School: Fresh, Mineral Style

San Gimignano modern school

Panizzi: the flagship Vernaccia di San Gimignano Riserva, stainless steel + very brief oak contact, keeping floral freshness and a mineral outline while adding subtle depth. One of the most balanced interpretations of the grape.

Traditional School: Complex, Oak-Aged Style

San Gimignano traditional school

Montenidoli: Elisabetta Fagiuoli holds to traditional methods: Tradizionale is skin-macerated and Carato is aged in oak, giving wines with beeswax, nuts and mature complexity. Vernaccia's most characterful interpretation, for advanced lovers of complex aged whites.

Natural School: Low-Intervention Interpretations

San Gimignano natural school

Natural producers: some small growers use wild yeasts, no (or very low) added sulphur and skin contact, letting Vernaccia show natural orange-wine traits — a copper-gold colour, oxidative beeswax and orange-peel aromas. Vernaccia's most avant-garde experiment within the natural-wine movement.

Vernaccia vs Verdicchio: Style Comparison

Vernaccia: slightly bitter finish (almond skin), strong minerality, the saline character of San Gimignano's marine sandy soils
Verdicchio di Matelica: crisp high acidity, fresh green apple, a bitter-almond finish; the cool climate of the Marche hills gives a tighter acid structure
In common: both finish with bitter almond, and both can reach ageing complexity comparable to Pinot Gris or Chenin Blanc
slides.3.title: Ciliegiolo — From Supporting Role to Lead
slides.3.content:
A Name Meaning "Little Cherry"

The name Ciliegiolo (Italian for "little cherry") directly describes its core flavour — vivid wild sour cherry and wild strawberry. It long served as a supporting grape in Chianti blends (adding roundness to Sangiovese), but in recent years more and more producers on the Maremma coast (Maremma Toscana) and in Umbria have started making it as a varietal wine, revealing unexpected depth.

Main areas: Maremma Toscana DOC (coastal hills), Umbria / southern Toscana | Change of role: supporting → lead

Grape Profile and Winemaking Styles

Core aromas: wild sour cherry, wild strawberry, rose petal, violet | medium tannin, crisp acidity, light to medium body
Two interpretations: traditional heavy oak (12-18 months in French oak, a weightier structure) vs modern light-touch (stainless steel or large casks, keeping bright fruit)
Champions: estates such as Sassotondo (Maremma, single vineyard San Lorenzo) and Leonardo Bussoletti (Narni, Umbria) make Ciliegiolo their core grape; low intervention lets the wild berries burst out — a perfect summer red

Its Traditional Role in Chianti

The traditional Chianti formula (proposed by Baron Bettino Ricasoli in the 19th century): mainly Sangiovese, supported by Canaiolo, with a little Malvasia; Ciliegiolo was also often used as a supporting grape adding round fruit
Today Chianti Classico may be 100% Sangiovese, but estates' own old-vine Ciliegiolo has become important raw material for varietal wines
slides.4.title: Cesanese del Piglio — The Red Soul of Rome
slides.4.content:
A Table Wine of the Papal Court and Roman Nobility

History: records of the Cesanese grape go back to Roman times, and it is said to have been loved by popes and the Roman nobility. Today Cesanese del Piglio DOCG (2008) is Lazio's first DOCG and its only red DOCG (the other two are Frascati's white DOCGs)
Area: the village of Piglio in the province of Frosinone (about 60 km south-east of Rome), Apennine foothills | elevation 300-600 m

Grape Profile

Two sub-varieties: Cesanese di Affile (wilder, higher acidity) and Cesanese Comune (rounder, easier drinking)
Core aromas: blackberry, raspberry, violet, black pepper, tobacco leaf
Palate: medium-high tannin, medium-high acidity, full body | dry or lightly sweet or sparkling
Ageing: dry Riserva can reach 8-12 years

Roman Trattoria Culture

Food-pairing tradition: the house wine (vino della casa) of a traditional Roman trattoria is often Cesanese, served with Cacio e Pepe (cheese-and-pepper pasta), Carbonara, Supplì (fried rice balls) and other Roman dishes
Modern premiumisation: estates such as Coletti Conti and Casale della Ioria have recently pushed Cesanese upmarket, into Rome's high-end restaurants

The Appellations Compared

Cesanese del Piglio DOCG (2008): Lazio's only red DOCG, the most refined style
Cesanese di Affile DOC: a smaller area using the Cesanese di Affile variety, a wilder, more rustic style
Cesanese di Olevano Romano DOC: near Rome, mainly easy-drinking volume wines
Top producers: Coletti Conti (Romanico), Casale della Ioria (Torre del Piano)
slides.5.title: Colorino and Toscana's Traditional Blending System
slides.5.content:
The "Hidden Colourist" of Italian Wine

Colorino (Italian for "the one that gives colour") lives up to its name — its skins are extremely dark and very high in anthocyanins, giving wine an almost purple-black colour. It is almost never made on its own, but acts as the "colourist" of Chianti blends, giving them deeper colour and firmer tannic structure at 5-10% of the blend. It is one of the most low-key yet indispensable supporting players in Italian wine.

Role: supporting grape in Chianti blends | Area: all of Toscana | Style: dark, high tannin, high anthocyanins

Rare Grapes in Toscana's Traditional Blending System

Colorino del Valdarno: a member of the old traditional Chianti formula, grown mainly in the Arno valley (Valdarno), known for its concentrated purple-black colour and rich anthocyanins
Canaiolo: another traditional supporting grape, complementing Sangiovese with roundness and fruit; it once held a 15% share in Bettino Ricasoli's 19th-century Chianti formula, and its plantings have shrunk greatly today
Mammolo: a rare Tuscan grape with violet aromas (Mammolo = violet), occasionally blended into Vino Nobile di Montepulciano-based blends for floral lift; one of the Tuscan grapes closest to extinction
In summary: Toscana's traditional blending system relied on a dozen or so rare native grapes, each with its job — colour, aroma, acidity and tannin each came from different grapes. Since modern rules were relaxed, the push for Sangiovese alone has sharply reduced plantings of these supporting grapes, making their conservation important
slides.6.title: Central Italy's Rare Grapes Compared
slides.6.content:
Vernaccia di San Gimignano

White | DOCG | Italy's first DOC, 1966

Slightly bitter almond finish / strong minerality / fresh but can age 5-10 years (Riserva) / with white meat, seafood, truffle dishes

Ciliegiolo

Red | Maremma Toscana DOC / Umbria

Core aroma of wild sour cherry / light to medium body / a perfect summer red / a natural-wine darling

Cesanese del Piglio

Red | DOCG (2008) | Lazio's only red DOCG

Blackberry + black pepper + violet / said to have been loved by the papal court / emblem of Roman trattoria culture / dry Riserva ages 8-12 years

Colorino / traditional blending grapes

Red | all of Toscana / blending support

Deep colour + high anthocyanins / never made alone (5-10% of the blend) / gives Chianti depth of colour / at risk of shrinking plantings
slides.7.title: Key Takeaways
slides.7.points.0: Vernaccia di San Gimignano: Italy's first DOC in 1966 (DOCG in 1993); a slightly bitter almond finish + minerality is the grape's fingerprint; from San Gimignano, the town of stone towers
slides.7.points.1: Three schools of Vernaccia: modern (Panizzi, fresh and mineral), traditional (Montenidoli, oak and oxidative complexity), natural (small growers, skin-contact orange wine)
slides.7.points.2: Vernaccia vs Verdicchio: both finish with bitter almond; Vernaccia is more mineral, Verdicchio higher in acid and tighter
slides.7.points.3: Ciliegiolo: Italian for "little cherry", core aroma of wild sour cherry; traditionally a supporting grape in Chianti, recently promoted to lead by natural-leaning estates
slides.7.points.4: Cesanese del Piglio DOCG (2008): Lazio's first and only red DOCG, said to have been loved by the papal court, emblem of Roman trattoria wine culture; perfect with Cacio e Pepe / Carbonara
slides.7.points.5: Colorino (the colourist): deep purple-black colour + high anthocyanins, never made alone, giving Chianti depth of colour at 5-10%
slides.7.points.6: Toscana's traditional blending system: Colorino (colour) + Canaiolo (roundness) + Mammolo (violet aroma) each had a job, and face disappearance after modernisation
slides.7.points.7: Food: Vernaccia with lobster risotto / Ciliegiolo with tomato salad and roast chicken / Cesanese with Cacio e Pepe / Colorino blends with lamb chops
slides.8.title: Central Italy Rare Grapes Knowledge Check
slides.8.questions.0.question: What special place does Vernaccia di San Gimignano hold in Italian wine law?
slides.8.questions.0.options.2: The first Italian white to enter the US market
slides.8.questions.0.explanation: Vernaccia di San Gimignano became Italy's first DOC wine in 1966 and was promoted to DOCG in 1993 — a milestone in Italian wine law.
slides.8.questions.1.question: What is the signature flavour of Vernaccia di San Gimignano?
slides.8.questions.1.options.1: A slightly bitter finish (almond skin) and minerality
slides.8.questions.1.explanation: Vernaccia di San Gimignano's most recognisable fingerprint is a slightly bitter finish (almond skin) and a mineral aftertaste, linked to the particular mineral character of San Gimignano's soils.
slides.8.questions.2.question: What does the name Ciliegiolo mean, and what is its core aroma?
slides.8.questions.2.options.1: "Little olive", known for an oily texture
slides.8.questions.2.options.2: "Little cherry", known for wild sour cherry and rose
slides.8.questions.2.explanation: Ciliegiolo means "little cherry" in Italian; its core aromas are vivid wild sour cherry and strawberry with rose petal, making it one of Italy's most aromatic red grapes.
slides.8.questions.3.question: What is the historic and cultural standing of Cesanese del Piglio DOCG?
slides.8.questions.3.options.0: Toscana's oldest wine, emblem of the Florentine Republic
slides.8.questions.3.options.1: Said to have been loved by the papal court; Lazio's only red DOCG
slides.8.questions.3.options.2: Northern Italy's most representative red grape
slides.8.questions.3.options.3: The main export red of Venice's trading era
slides.8.questions.3.explanation: Cesanese del Piglio DOCG (2008) is Lazio's only red DOCG; historically it is said to have been loved by the papal court and Roman nobility, and it is still the soul red of Roman trattorias.
slides.8.questions.4.question: What is the main function of Colorino in Chianti blends?
slides.8.questions.4.options.1: Giving deep colour and rich anthocyanins
slides.8.questions.4.explanation: Colorino (Italian for "the one that gives colour") is known for very high anthocyanins and a deep purple-black colour; at 5-10% it gives Chianti depth of colour, and it is Italian wine's most important "colourist" grape.
slides.8.questions.5.question: Why did the natural-wine movement help raise Ciliegiolo's standing?
slides.8.questions.5.options.1: Low-intervention winemaking lets Ciliegiolo's wild-berry character show fully, promoting it from supporting role to lead
slides.8.questions.5.options.2: The movement won Ciliegiolo DOCG status
slides.8.questions.5.options.3: The movement drove Ciliegiolo prices up sharply
slides.8.questions.5.explanation: Natural wine favours low intervention, letting the grape's personality lead the style — Ciliegiolo's bright wild berries and rose stand out especially under low intervention, moving it from a Chianti supporting grape to a varietal lead.
slides.8.questions.6.question: Which Central Italian white grape is known for a "bitter-almond finish" and a "cool upland high-acid structure", making it the counterpart to Vernaccia?
slides.8.questions.6.explanation: Verdicchio di Matelica comes from the hills of the Marche and is known for crisp high acidity, fresh green apple and a bitter-almond finish. One of Central Italy's most important white grapes, it echoes Vernaccia's slightly bitter finish but in a tighter style.
